name: Experimental Design Common Pitfalls
description: This module lists frequently observed mistakes, bugs, and anti-patterns seen in everyday experimental design work, so they can be recognized and avoided during typical experimental design tasks.
content:
This module lists frequently observed mistakes, bugs, and anti-patterns seen in everyday experimental design work, so they can be recognized and avoided during typical experimental design tasks.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. Re-check edge cases relevant to experimental design (empty input, boundary values, concurrent access) before calling the task done.
2. When experimental design guidance conflicts with a specific user instruction, defer to the user's explicit instruction and note the conflict.
3. Check that experimental design terminology is used consistently throughout, matching existing conventions in the surrounding context.
4. State assumptions about experimental design explicitly before proceeding, rather than leaving them implicit.
5. When experimental design decisions are ambiguous, favor the option that is easiest to reverse or extend later.
6. When multiple experimental design strategies are viable, name the trade-off explicitly rather than silently picking one.
7. Document any non-obvious experimental design decision with a short rationale so future readers understand the 'why', not just the 'what'.
8. Prefer explicit, readable experimental design solutions over clever ones that are hard to verify.
9. Prefer the simplest experimental design approach that satisfies the requirement over a more general one that isn't needed yet.
10. Keep experimental design changes scoped to what was asked; avoid unrelated cleanup in the same pass.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Do not treat a single passing example as full verification of experimental design correctness.
- Do not silently drop experimental design edge cases to make an example look cleaner than the real system.
- Avoid introducing new experimental design abstractions before there is a second concrete use case that needs them.

CLOSING NOTE
These guidelines are a starting point for experimental design, not an exhaustive rulebook — use judgment when a rule doesn't fit the situation.
